germany-smuggling-gangs-operation.headline: Germany targets Channel-crossing smuggling gangs from secret police operation
germany-smuggling-gangs-operation.body_md:
German federal police have opened a window onto one of their longest-running efforts against the smuggling networks that supply small boats for Channel crossings, disclosing details of an intelligence-gathering operation built around the warehouses where dinghies, outboard motors and life jackets are staged before being driven to the French coast. The disclosure, described to the BBC, marks a rare moment of visibility into an enforcement effort that has typically stayed out of view.

Germany has functioned for years as the back office of the Channel smuggling trade. Essen, a mid-sized city in the Ruhr valley, became notorious after a 2024 BBC undercover investigation found smugglers openly advertising "packages" — an inflatable boat, a motor and 60 life jackets — for around €15,000, stored across what smugglers themselves said were roughly ten warehouses in the area, spread out deliberately so that a single police raid would not shut down the business.

## A loophole closes

That resilience was, until recently, partly a function of German law. Storing boats destined for a country outside the EU — the UK, after Brexit — was not itself a crime, which meant police could seize equipment but struggled to prosecute the organisers who owned it. That changed on 19 December 2025, when the Bundestag passed legislation, negotiated as part of a broader security arrangement between Sir Keir Starmer and Chancellor Friedrich Merz, making the storage and onward supply of boats and engines for Channel crossings a criminal offence carrying sentences of up to ten years.

![A German federal police patrol car](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/28/Streifenwagen_Bundespolizei.jpg)

The new law gave the Bundespolizei a legal basis to build cases the way they would against organised crime more broadly — through sustained surveillance rather than one-off raids on tip-offs. That shift appears to be the backdrop to this week's disclosure: an intelligence operation that has been tracking the warehouse network's suppliers, financing and internal logistics over time, rather than simply waiting for a shipment to move.

## A pattern of joint raids

The operation sits alongside a string of joint actions this year. In March, close to 1,000 officers — including the GSG9 tactical unit — carried out dawn raids across four German states, hitting more than two dozen properties tied to a network moving migrants from the Middle East and East Africa. In May, a further raid in North Rhine-Westphalia, run with Britain's National Crime Agency, seized more than 30 boats, 20 engines and 9,000 life jackets. Each operation has chipped away at capacity without stopping the trade: French officials reported a single dinghy carrying 230 people crossing the Channel earlier this month, evidence that smugglers are adapting by packing more people onto fewer boats rather than reducing the number of crossings.

## Why the disclosure matters

German police rarely narrate their intelligence work in public, and doing so now reads as a signal — to smuggling networks and to London — that Berlin intends to use its new legal powers rather than let them sit unused. For the UK, it reinforces a security relationship that has become one of the few tangible outputs of the post-Brexit reset with Germany. What it does not yet show is results: no arrest figures or prosecution timeline under the new law have been disclosed alongside the operation.

The next marker will be whether German prosecutors bring the first cases under the December statute, and whether the Bundestag, which has been criticised for slow follow-through on the Starmer-Merz accord, keeps pace with the enforcement side. Channel crossing numbers for the current season, due from the Home Office in the coming weeks, will show whether any of this activity is denting the flow.

anthropic-q2-revenue-ipo.headline: Anthropic Q2 revenue hits $11.5bn, up 14x year-on-year, as fall IPO looms
anthropic-q2-revenue-ipo.body_md:
Anthropic told prospective investors this month that its revenue more than doubled in the second quarter of 2026, crossing $11.5bn, and that the company turned an operating profit for the first time — a claim that, if it holds up, would mark one of the fastest climbs to profitable scale any technology company has managed.

The figures were not announced by Anthropic itself. They come from internal documents shared with investors ahead of a planned autumn stock listing, first reported by Bloomberg News and since corroborated by the Wall Street Journal and multiple outlets including CNBC and Fortune. Anthropic has declined to comment officially, and the company's own disclosures describe the numbers as preliminary — "deliberations are ongoing and the figures could be revised," as Bloomberg's sourcing put it.

Even with that caveat, the trajectory is striking. Anthropic's revenue is reported to have gone from around $787m in the second quarter of 2025 to $4.73bn in the first quarter of this year to more than $11.5bn in the second — a roughly 14-fold year-on-year jump and more than double the prior quarter. The company's annualised run rate, a separate measure derived from a given month's revenue multiplied by twelve, was already put at $47bn back in May.

![Dario Amodei, Anthropic's co-founder and chief executive, speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt in September 2023](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e4/Dario_Amodei_at_TechCrunch_Disrupt_2023_01_%28cropped%29.jpg)

## Where the money is coming from

The growth is not evenly spread. Enterprise adoption of Claude Code, Anthropic's coding assistant, has been the standout driver — the product alone is reported to have reached roughly $8bn in annualised revenue by May, with customers including Netflix, Spotify and Salesforce, and business subscriptions said to have quadrupled since the start of the year. More than 1,000 customers now reportedly spend over $1m a year with Anthropic, doubling in barely two months this spring. That is the pattern behind the topline number: this is not a single blockbuster product but an API and coding business compounding across a widening enterprise customer base.

The positive operating income is the more consequential claim. Frontier AI labs have spent the past three years burning enormous sums on compute and training runs, and investors have generally been asked to take profitability on faith, years out. An operating profit — even a modest, "adjusted" one, which typically excludes items like stock compensation — would be the first hard evidence that the economics of running large language models at scale can turn positive before a company burns through its balance sheet entirely.

## The IPO backdrop

The numbers are surfacing now because Anthropic is deep in preparation for a stock market listing, with Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan Chase working the offering and a confidential filing already lodged with the SEC in June. Investor meetings have been under way since July, and reports this week suggest bankers and existing investors are discussing a listing as soon as September or October at a valuation approaching $2 trillion — roughly double the $965bn price tag set in May's $65bn Series H round, and enough to make it the largest IPO on record, ahead of SpaceX's $1.77 trillion debut in June.

That valuation is where the skepticism concentrates. A $2 trillion price tag, at typical Nasdaq-100 multiples, would imply Anthropic needs to be generating something in the range of $60bn-$80bn in annual net profit to look fairly priced — a figure nowhere close to what even the most bullish reading of this quarter's numbers implies. Amazon, held up as the scale comparison bankers are reportedly using, made $200.6bn in revenue and $62.6bn in net income in its own second quarter this year. Anthropic's reported operating profit, whatever its size, is not the same thing as net income, and the company has not disclosed one.

## What to watch

None of this is yet a matter of public record. Anthropic has filed confidentially, which means the figures investors are currently working from — including this quarter's revenue and profit claims — will not be independently auditable until a public S-1 is released, expected in the coming weeks if the September or October timeline holds. That filing, not this week's leaks, is the point at which the $11.5bn claim either becomes a verified data point or gets revised. Rival OpenAI, which had also eyed a fall listing, is now reportedly looking at 2027 instead — leaving Anthropic to make its case to public markets largely on its own.

**In one sentence:** Anthropic told IPO investors its revenue passed $11.5bn last quarter with its first operating profit, but the numbers are unaudited and the $2tn valuation being floated implies profits it hasn't shown.

uk-solar-record-july.headline: UK solar power hit record 14.4% of electricity generation in July
uk-solar-record-july.body_md:
Solar panels supplied a record 14.4% of Great Britain's electricity in July, according to figures compiled by National Energy System Operator (NESO) and highlighted by industry body Solar Energy UK — the highest monthly share the technology has ever achieved on the grid.

The figure beats the previous record of 12.4%, set just two months earlier in May, and is well over half again the 9.6% solar managed in July 2025. Panels generated 3.2 terawatt-hours of electricity over the month, according to Energy UK data cited by trade press — enough, roughly, to supply 1.28 million homes for a year.

![Solar panels arrayed across a UK field near the Great Ouse](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/20/Solar_Farm_by_the_Great_Ouse_-_geograph.org.uk_-_7096522.jpg)

## A sunny month, and a fast-growing fleet

Two forces did the work. July was exceptionally bright — England and Wales recorded their sunniest calendar month since Met Office records began, at roughly twice the seasonal average — and the amount of solar capacity connected to the grid kept climbing. Britain added 142,536 new solar installations between January and July, the strongest first-half figure since 2011, when a wave of subsidy-driven rooftop fitting swept the country. Most of this year's additions were domestic rooftop systems rather than utility-scale farms, spreading the capacity gain across millions of individual meters rather than a handful of large sites.

The monthly record had a sharper peak inside it. On Sunday 12 July, solar supplied 18.8% of the day's generation — just shy of the single-day record of 19.5% set on 24 May — and in the two hours either side of midday it briefly accounted for 44% of everything flowing onto the grid. Those windows illustrate both the promise and the awkwardness of solar's growth: for a couple of hours a fine summer weekend can look like a genuinely post-fossil grid, and for the other twenty-two it cannot.

"The more solar we generate, the less exposed families and households are to energy price shocks," said Michael Shanks, the UK's energy minister, in comments reported alongside the figures. Chris Hewett, chief executive of Solar Energy UK, put the shift in longer perspective: fifteen years ago, he said, solar was "a footnote in the electricity mix," and it is now "a major player" delivering "home-grown, cheap, clean and reliable energy."

## Why the grid, not just the panels, matters now

The more interesting question is no longer whether solar can be built fast enough — the installation numbers answer that — but whether the system built to absorb it can keep pace. NESO has already logged a string of new instantaneous output records this year, including a peak of over 15,400 megawatts, alongside stretches of near-zero or negative wholesale prices when solar and wind output has swamped demand. Negative pricing is a signal that supply is temporarily outrunning what the grid can usefully do with it, whether through storage, exports or flexible demand — not a one-off curiosity but a symptom that will recur more often as capacity keeps rising.

Renewables supplied 52.1% of Britain's electricity across 2025, up from around 3% in 2000, and solar has gone from roughly a thirtieth of that renewable capacity fifteen years ago to about a third of it today. Solar Energy UK forecasts a further 5 to 5.5 gigawatts of new capacity this year. Each increment adds pressure on network operators to manage curtailment, storage and grid balancing — the unglamorous plumbing that determines whether record generation months translate into cheaper, more reliable power or simply into wasted output on the sunniest days.

## What's next

Attention now turns to whether August, historically a strong solar month, can extend the run, and to how NESO manages the balancing costs that come with it. The next test of scale arrives with October's Energy Trends release from the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, which will show whether July's surge was a summer spike or a step change in solar's underlying share of the mix.

man-city-bouaddi-fernandez.headline: Man City move for £85m-rated Bouaddi while still pursuing Fernandez
man-city-bouaddi-fernandez.body_md:
Manchester City's midfield has been gutted this summer, and the club's response is to spend its way back to full strength — fast.

Rodri, the Ballon d'Or winner who anchored City's midfield for six years, is completing a move to Barcelona worth up to £65m. Tijjani Reijnders, signed only last year, is also on his way out. Bernardo Silva has already left for Real Madrid. That is three midfield departures in one window, and new manager Enzo Maresca — who succeeded Pep Guardiola at the end of June — is trying to fill the gap with two of Europe's most sought-after names before the deadline on 1 September.

![Ayyoub Bouaddi playing for Morocco against Norway, June 2026](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Ayyoub_Bouaddi_Morocco_v_Norway_7_June_2026-71_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Ayyoub_Bouaddi_Morocco_v_Norway_7_June_2026-71_%28cropped%29.jpg)

## The teenager City are chasing

The more advanced deal is for Ayyoub Bouaddi, the 18-year-old Lille midfielder who lit up this summer's World Cup for Morocco, the country he switched allegiance to from France in May. Lille value him at around £85m — a startling figure for a player who only turned 18 in October — and Bouaddi has reportedly made clear he wants the move. City are said to have agreed five-year contract terms with him, with talks over a fee entering their final stages.

Lille's manager, Davide Ancelotti, has not hidden his reluctance to sell. "There is interest from so many clubs," he said. "He is a really, really good player and I hope that he is going to stay with us." He added: "He's going to be one of the best midfielders in Europe for the next 10 years" — the kind of endorsement that tends to precede a departure rather than prevent one.

## The one that got away — for now

City's other target is further from the finish line. Enzo Fernández, Chelsea's Argentina World Cup winner, has 16 goals and 10 assists to his name from last season and has made clear he wants to leave Stamford Bridge. City tabled a £102.5m bid, short of Chelsea's £120m valuation, and then missed a Friday deadline Chelsea had set for a full-price offer. Chelsea now insist he will not be sold this window or in January.

That is not quite the end of it. City retain the option to return with an improved bid in the window's final fortnight, and Fernández's relationship with Maresca from their time together at Chelsea gives the pursuit some logic beyond the transfer sheet. Asked directly about him this week, Maresca kept it neutral: "It's a player from another club." City have also been linked with Liverpool's Alexis Mac Allister as an alternative should Fernández prove unreachable.

## What it says about City's summer

Taken together, the two pursuits are less a transfer story than a repair job. Losing Rodri, Reijnders and Bernardo Silva in a single window would strain any midfield, City's included, and the club's response — chase a generational teenage prospect and a proven Premier League performer at the same time — is as much about hedging as ambition. Whether either deal lands before the window shuts will say a good deal about how City manage a squad rebuild without their long-serving manager for the first time in a decade.

The next marker is 1 September. Bouaddi's move looks the more likely to close first; Fernández's depends on whether Chelsea's resolve holds once City decide how much more they are willing to pay.

liv-golf-cancels-finale.headline: LIV Golf cancels season finale to regroup for 'next chapter'
liv-golf-cancels-finale.body_md:
LIV Golf has pulled the plug on its own season finale — a $40 million team championship that was due to tee off in Michigan on 27 August — and will instead close out 2026 this week at a tournament outside Indianapolis that was never meant to be the last word.

![LIV Golf logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/12/Liv_golf.jpg)

It is the second event the Saudi-backed circuit has scrapped this year, after a $30 million stop in New Orleans was axed in June. Players were told of the Michigan cancellation midweek and, according to several who spoke to The Telegraph, still don't know whether the $40 million in team prize money will be paid out at all. LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil framed the decision as tactical rather than terminal: "By concluding the season now, we can put our full resources behind what comes next and maintain the operational rigor this transition demands." He added that the league would carry fan "energy and enthusiasm... into what comes next" — the vague but recurring phrase, "the next chapter of LIV Golf," doing a lot of work to paper over a fairly stark financial picture.

## A fund walking away, quietly

That picture: Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, which has bankrolled LIV since its 2022 launch with reported annual outlays in the hundreds of millions, told the league in April it would stop financing the tour once the 2026 season ends. O'Neil has since said LIV has struck an agreement with an unnamed "lead investor" to fund 2027, with terms expected to be finalised later this month, and claims "strong interest from more than a dozen additional parties" in taking minority stakes. What that leaves is a golf tour designed around nine-figure PIF cheques now shopping for outside capital mid-transition — not the posture of an operation confident enough to run its full calendar.

The restructuring already has a name: LIV 2.0. Ten events instead of fourteen, split evenly between domestic and international stops, with purses trimmed from the $30 million-plus norm. In exchange, players are being offered something they didn't have before — commercial rights to their own names and likenesses, and majority equity in the league itself. It reads less like a growth plan and more like PIF converting a subsidy into a smaller, player-owned entity it can step back from without simply shutting the lights off.

## The merger that isn't happening

The cancellation lands ten days after PGA Tour commissioner Brian Rolapp closed off the question that has hovered over golf since 2023. "There's no merger, no conversations," he told Bloomberg on 7 August, adding the Tour was "really concentrated" on its own product rather than any tie-up with the Saudi-financed rival. That flatly contradicts any read of this week's news as a step toward reunification — if anything, it suggests LIV is retrenching to survive independently rather than positioning itself for a deal Rolapp has just ruled out. The Asian Tour's recent alignment with the PGA Tour and DP World Tour, which cuts off one of LIV's remaining recruitment pipelines, only tightens the squeeze.

What happens next is mundane by comparison to the drama: LIV's Indianapolis-area event this week crowns the 2026 team champion by default, the new lead-investor deal is due to close before year-end, and the ten-event LIV 2.0 slate needs a schedule, sponsors and broadcast homes before it can claim to be a fresh start rather than a smaller version of the same uncertainty.

labour-mp-suspended-covid-loan.headline: Labour MP suspended amid investigation into Covid loan scheme
labour-mp-suspended-covid-loan.body_md:
Bayo Alaba, the Labour MP for Southend East and Rochford, has had the whip suspended after referring himself to his own party for investigation over a taxpayer-backed pandemic loan. The move — unusual in that Alaba triggered it himself rather than waiting to be caught — followed questions from The Times about a £50,000 Bounce Back Loan taken out by Alaba Properties Ltd, a business he co-owns.

![Bayo Alaba, MP for Southend East and Rochford](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b4/Official_portrait_of_Bayo_Alaba_MP_2024_Crop_2.jpg)

The loan was the maximum available under the Bounce Back scheme, the emergency lending programme that let small businesses borrow up to £50,000 with minimal checks and a state guarantee covering the full amount if the borrower defaulted. Companies House records show an attempt was made to dissolve Alaba Properties in March 2022 — a company can only be struck off if it has no outstanding debts, so a wind-up attempt while a loan remains unpaid invites scrutiny. Alaba has since said one of two loans he took out has been settled, and insists there was "no attempt to avoid my financial obligations."

## Self-referral, then suspension

A Labour spokesperson said the party "expects the highest standards from our elected representatives" and has "robust processes in place" to enforce them, declining further comment while the investigation proceeds. Alaba, elected in 2024 on an 18.9-point swing that unseated two decades of Conservative representation in Southend, has agreed to administrative suspension from the party pending the outcome, and the whip has been withdrawn — meaning he now sits in the Commons as an independent rather than as a Labour MP, though he keeps his seat. The party stressed the process is being run without prejudice, implying no finding of wrongdoing at this stage.

Mike Wood, the shadow Cabinet Office minister, was blunter, telling The Times that Alaba "clearly has questions to answer." Alaba himself has largely declined to elaborate publicly beyond his initial statement.

## Not an isolated case

Alaba's is the second British case this year of an MP losing the whip over Bounce Back Loan questions. In May, Reform UK's James McMurdock removed himself from his party's whip after The Sunday Times reported he had borrowed £70,000 across two companies — one of which, by his own turnover, would not plausibly have qualified for the sum. Neither firm appeared to have significant staff or trading history at the time the loans were issued.

The scheme that both cases trace back to was designed for speed, not scrutiny — self-certified turnover figures, no credit checks, money out within days — because the alternative in April 2020 was to watch viable businesses collapse for want of a bridging loan. That trade-off produced roughly £47 billion in lending and, by the National Audit Office's estimates, several billion pounds in losses to fraud and default, much of it never recovered. The scheme's design flaws are well documented; what is less common is seeing them surface in the political class doing the governing rather than the small businesses the scheme was built for.

## What happens next

Labour's internal investigation has no published timeline, and there is no indication either case has yet reached the level of a police referral or Insolvency Service inquiry — the routes through which most Bounce Back fraud has actually been pursued. The more immediate marker to watch is whether Alaba is readmitted to the parliamentary party, loses it for good, or — as happened with several MPs suspended over other conduct issues in 2024 — the process simply runs quietly for months without resolution.

amazon-mgm-uk-studio-expansion.headline: Amazon MGM wins UK film commission backing for studio expansion
amazon-mgm-uk-studio-expansion.body_md:
Amazon MGM Studios wants to more than double the sound stage capacity of Bray Film Studios, the Berkshire lot where Hammer Films once churned out Dracula sequels and where Amazon now shoots *The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power*. The plan — six new sound stages, four workshop buildings, a multi-storey car park and a production office inside a Grade II-listed former mansion — would take the site's stage space to roughly 20,000 square metres, enough for Amazon to run two big productions side by side. The Royal Borough of Windsor and Maidenhead is due to rule on the application, filed in July, this autumn.

![Bray Film Studios on the banks of the Thames, Berkshire](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/32/Bray_Film_Studios_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1591972.jpg)

What makes this more than a planning story is the backing behind it. The British Film Commission — the public-private body tasked with pitching Britain to Hollywood — counts Bray among its studio partners and has given the Amazon MGM productions filmed there, including *Rings of Power*, bespoke support in navigating UK infrastructure and permitting. Ministers have leaned in too: when Amazon confirmed the Bray purchase, the government welcomed it as proof of Britain's pull as "Europe's top filmmaking destination." Amazon puts the jobs number at around 3,200 across the UK, with 1,700 in Berkshire and 470 during construction alone.

## The subsidy underneath the sound stages

None of this happens in a vacuum. Since April 2025, UK productions have qualified for the Audio-Visual Expenditure Credit at 25.5%, with visual-effects spend now stripped of the usual 80% expenditure cap and topped up with a further 3.75% uplift — one of the most generous VFX incentives anywhere. UK film and high-end TV spend hit £6.8 billion in 2025, up 22% on the year, and Disney has been the single largest beneficiary of Britain's tax relief regime over the past 15 years. Amazon's Bray bet sits squarely inside that pattern: a US streamer converting a favourable tax and planning environment into permanent bricks and steel, rather than a one-off shoot.

## The dependency question

The same trend has a harder edge. The Commons Culture, Media and Sport Committee has flagged that Britain's reliance on US inward investment is "not without risk" — a warning borne out in 2023, when the Hollywood writers' and actors' strikes cut UK high-end TV investment by 49% and film by 35% almost overnight. Academics at the University of Reading have separately argued that Hollywood money has pushed studio and crew costs beyond what domestic broadcasters can afford, squeezing out British-financed film and TV even as the big US-backed productions thrive. A permanent Amazon campus at Bray is a vote of confidence in that system holding — but it also means more of Britain's production capacity is tied to a single overseas studio's slate, and to a tax credit regime that could yet be reshaped by a future chancellor.

The Windsor and Maidenhead planning committee's autumn decision is the next formal checkpoint; Thames Valley Police have already raised objections over a proposed second site access that will need resolving first.
